questions.prompt: Put the improvement loop in order.
questions.explain: A fix starts with noticing the problem, and a baseline measurement makes the fix trustworthy.
items: Notice the agent did the wrong thing and save the prompt
Write or edit a Skill that steers it
Run the prompt with and without the Skill, several times each
Compare the two and keep, fix or drop the Skill

questions.prompt: A Skill scores 100% with it and 100% without it. What does that tell you?
questions.explain: The measure is the difference. No difference means the Skill adds nothing for this case, perhaps because the model already does it.

options.text: For this case the Skill adds nothing you can measure
The Skill is excellent and should be kept as it is
options.misconception: A high score both ways means the model passes without help, so the Skill is not responsible.

options.text: The eval is proven correct, since everything passes
options.misconception: An always-passing check may be too easy. Read raw outputs before trusting it.

options.text: The model is too strong to be given Skills at all
options.misconception: It only says this case is easy. Harder cases may still show a difference.

questions.prompt: You ran each arm once and the Skill arm was better. What is wrong with stopping there?
questions.explain: Output varies between runs, so a single pair can be luck. Repeat the runs before concluding.

options.text: One run each cannot separate the effect from random variation
Nothing, since a better result is simply a better result
options.misconception: Models vary between runs, so one better run can be chance.

options.text: Evals are only valid when they are run on a shared cluster
options.misconception: The number of runs is what matters here.

questions.prompt: Check the result, or check the process?
questions.explain: Result checks look at what was produced. Process checks look at how the agent got there, such as whether the Skill was used.

items.text: The output file exists and has the expected header
items.misconception: This looks at what was produced.

items.text: The Skill was invoked at least once during the run
items.misconception: This looks at how the agent worked, not at the output.

items.text: The reported record count matches a count you made yourself
items.misconception: This compares the produced answer to ground truth.

questions.prompt: Which kind of grader fits each check best?
questions.explain: Use a script when the rule is exact, a person when the call is about real quality, and a judge model for open-ended text at a scale a person cannot read.

items.text: The output file exists and its header has 5 columns
items.misconception: This is an exact rule a script can check for free, with the same answer every time.

items.text: Does this summary of a paper's methods read as accurate to someone who knows the field?
items.misconception: This needs expert judgement about real quality. A script cannot state it as a rule.

items.text: Marking 200 free-text answers against a written PASS/FAIL rubric
items.misconception: The answers are open-ended and too many to read by hand, so a judge model fits. It costs a call per mark, and you should still read a sample.

questions.prompt: Your evals passed last spring. A new model version is released. What do you do?
questions.explain: Models and tools change. Re-running the same evals shows whether the Skill still helps or has become unnecessary.

options.text: Re-run the evals, with and without
Keep trusting the old results, since the Skill itself has not changed
options.misconception: The Skill is one half of the comparison. The model is the other half, and it changed.

options.text: Delete the Skill, because a newer model never needs any Skill
options.misconception: Some Skills still help, such as lab-specific rules the model cannot know. Measure instead of assuming.

questions.prompt: A model grades 200 outputs from another model of the same family. What is the best check on the scores?
questions.explain: A same-family judge is not an independent grader. Check a sample by hand against reference answers written before you saw the outputs.

options.text: Check a sample by hand against answers fixed in advance
Accept the scores, since the judge understands that style of output
options.misconception: Models tend to favour output like their own, so agreement can reflect similarity, so a high score may not mean correctness.

options.text: Use a larger model of the same family and skip hand checks
options.misconception: A larger model from the same family is still not independent of the one being judged.

options.text: Write the reference answers after reading the outputs
options.misconception: References written afterwards drift towards what the outputs said. Fix them first.
